module: C6 Rate and Extent of Reactions

Rate of Reaction.intro: The rate of a reaction measures how quickly reactants are converted to products. It can be measured by how quickly a reactant is used up or a product is formed.
Rate of Reaction.mnemonic: Rate = change ÷ time. Think of a CAR speeding: Concentration, Area (surface), Rate goes up with Temperature too! CART = Concentration, Area, Rate, Temperature.

sections.title: Measuring Rate
sections.text: Rate of reaction can be found by measuring how fast a reactant is used up or a product is formed over time.
points: Rate formula — Rate = amount of product formed (or reactant used) ÷ time taken
Gas syringe method — collect gas produced; record volume at intervals; plot volume vs time
Mass loss method — place on balance; record mass at intervals as gas escapes
Colorimetry/colour change — measure colour intensity as reactant is consumed
Disappearing cross method — time how long until a cross under the flask is no longer visible (precipitation)
Rate decreases over time — as reactants are used up, fewer collisions occur, so rate falls

sections.title: Rate from a Graph
sections.text: Rate-time graphs and concentration-time graphs both give information about how the rate changes during a reaction.
points: Steeper gradient — faster rate of reaction at that point
Flat line — reaction has stopped (reactant fully used up, not just slow)
Initial rate — steepest at the start; highest concentration of reactants
Tangent method — draw a tangent to the curve at the required point; gradient = rise ÷ run = rate
Mean rate — total change in quantity ÷ total time; gives an average, not instantaneous rate
Comparing experiments — steeper curve AND same final amount reached = faster rate, same amount of product

callout.label: Calculating Rate
callout.text: Draw a tangent to the curve at the point of interest. Rate = gradient = rise ÷ run. For mean rate: total change ÷ total time.

sections.title: Units and Calculations
sections.text: Understanding how to calculate and express rate correctly is essential for exam success.
points: Units of rate — depend on what is measured: cm³/s (gas volume), g/s (mass), mol/dm³/s (concentration)
Worked example — if 48 cm³ of gas is collected in 60 s: mean rate = 48 ÷ 60 = 0.8 cm³/s
Instantaneous rate — rate at one specific moment; found using a tangent to the curve
Mean rate — average over the whole reaction or a time interval
Comparing rates — steeper gradient = faster rate; a reaction finishing sooner does NOT mean it produced more product
Limiting reagent — the reactant that runs out first; determines when the reaction stops

keyTerms.def: The speed at which reactants are converted to products; measured as change in quantity per unit time
Total amount of change divided by total time taken — gives an average across the whole reaction
The rate at one specific moment in time — found by drawing a tangent to a concentration-time graph
A straight line that touches a curve at one point — its gradient gives the instantaneous rate
The reactant that is completely used up first, causing the reaction to stop
Reactions occur when particles collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy

examTips: Steeper gradient on a graph = faster rate. Always state this when comparing curves.
A flat line on a graph means the reaction is complete — not that it is slow. The limiting reagent has been used up.
Initial rate (start of graph) is always the fastest because reactant concentration is highest at the beginning.
When calculating mean rate, always specify the time interval: e.g. mean rate between 0 and 30 s = change in volume ÷ 30.
commonMistakes: Confusing a flat line (reaction complete, limiting reagent used up) with a slow rate — the reaction has stopped, not slowed.
Calculating mean rate instead of instantaneous rate when asked for the rate at a specific point — you must draw a tangent.
Mixing up the units of rate — check what is being measured (gas volume, mass, concentration) and use appropriate units per second.
clozePassages: The rate of reaction measures how quickly reactants are converted to products. It can be measured by monitoring the change in mass, volume of gas produced, or concentration of a reactant or product over time. Rate = change in quantity ÷ time. A steeper gradient on a graph means a faster rate. The rate decreases over time as reactants are used up and their concentration falls.

Reaction rates can be explained using collision theory. For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with sufficient energy — at least the activation energy. More frequent successful collisions lead to a faster reaction. Factors that increase the frequency or energy of collisions — such as increasing temperature, concentration, surface area, or adding a catalyst — all increase the rate of reaction.

The rate of reaction can be measured in several ways. If a gas is produced, its volume can be measured over time using a gas syringe. If a precipitate forms, the time taken for a cross to become obscured can be measured. The mass of the reaction flask can be measured if a gas escapes. Plotting mass or volume against time gives a curve that flattens when the reaction stops — at this point the limiting reagent is used up.

Factors Affecting Rate.intro: Several factors affect how quickly a reaction occurs. All explanations should be linked to collision theory.
Factors Affecting Rate.mnemonic: TESCP — Temperature, (surface) area, concentration, pressure, catalyst. Remember: 'Terrific Elephants Can't Possibly Stop' chemical reactions speeding up!

sections.title: Collision Theory
sections.text: For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy. More frequent, higher-energy collisions = faster rate.
points: Successful collision — particles must meet AND have energy ≥ activation energy
Activation energy — the minimum energy needed; if collision energy is below this, no reaction occurs
Frequency of collisions — more collisions per second = more chance of successful reactions
Energy of collisions — higher energy = more collisions exceed activation energy threshold
Particle size matters — smaller particles have greater surface area for collisions
Maxwell-Boltzmann — the distribution of kinetic energies in particles; only those above Ea react

sections.title: The Five Factors
sections.text: Five key factors can change the rate of a reaction — always link each one back to collision theory in exam answers.
points: Temperature — higher temp gives particles more kinetic energy; collide more frequently AND with more energy; a greater proportion exceed activation energy; rate increases significantly
Concentration (solutions) — more particles in the same volume; more frequent collisions per unit time
Pressure (gases) — same effect as concentration — particles are closer together, so collide more frequently
Surface area — smaller pieces (powder vs lumps) expose more particles at the surface; more frequent collisions
Catalyst — provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy; not consumed; more collisions are successful

sections.title: Catalysts in Detail
sections.text: Catalysts speed up reactions by providing a lower-energy route for the reaction, shown as a lower activation energy peak on an energy profile.
points: Lower activation energy — more particle collisions have sufficient energy to react
Not consumed — the catalyst is unchanged at the end of the reaction
Specific to reactions — different reactions require different catalysts
Industrial importance — iron in Haber process, vanadium pentoxide in Contact process, platinum in catalytic converters
Enzymes — biological catalysts; work at body temperature; e.g. amylase breaks down starch
Energy profile — catalysed pathway shown as a lower peak; ΔH of reaction is UNCHANGED

callout.label: Catalysts
callout.text: A catalyst lowers the activation energy — shown on an energy profile as a lower peak. It does NOT change the overall energy change (ΔH) or the equilibrium position.

keyTerms.def: Theory stating that reactions occur when particles collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
The minimum energy particles must have for a collision to result in a reaction
A substance that speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative lower-energy pathway; not used up in the reaction
The area of a solid exposed to reactants; greater surface area means more collisions and a faster rate
The amount of solute per unit volume; higher concentration means more particles in a given volume and more frequent collisions
A biological catalyst — a protein that speeds up a specific reaction in living organisms

examTips: Always explain using collision theory — don't just say 'more collisions'. State WHY: 'particles have more kinetic energy so collide more frequently AND with more energy, so more collisions exceed the activation energy'.
Catalyst lowers the activation energy — it does NOT affect the overall energy change (ΔH) or shift equilibrium position.
Temperature affects BOTH the frequency AND the energy of collisions — mention both in exam answers for full marks.
When asked to compare two experiments: state which is faster AND explain why using collision theory.
commonMistakes: Saying 'more collisions' without explaining why the factor causes this — always link to particle movement, concentration, or energy.
Thinking catalysts change the overall ΔH of the reaction — they only lower the activation energy.
Forgetting that catalysts are not used up — they are regenerated at the end and can be reused.
clozePassages: Temperature increases the rate of reaction because particles move faster, collide more frequently, and have more energy. A higher proportion of collisions exceed the activation energy. A 10°C rise in temperature approximately doubles the reaction rate. This is why food stored in a refrigerator lasts longer — the lower temperature reduces the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions in bacteria that cause food to spoil.

Concentration affects the rate of reaction. A higher concentration means more particles in a given volume, leading to more frequent collisions. Increasing concentration increases the probability of successful collisions per unit time. For reactions in solution, increasing the concentration of reactants increases the rate. For gaseous reactions, increasing pressure has the same effect as increasing concentration.

A catalyst increases the rate of reaction without being used up itself. It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful. Catalysts are specific — different reactions need different catalysts. Enzymes are biological catalysts. Industrial catalysts include iron in the Haber process and vanadium pentoxide in the Contact process. Catalysts are economically important as they reduce energy costs.

Equilibrium.intro: Some reactions are reversible — they can proceed in both directions. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations remain constant.
Equilibrium.mnemonic: Le Chatelier's Principle: 'If you STRESS the system, it will do its BEST to RESIST.' Higher temperature? It shifts to use up heat. More pressure? It shifts to reduce moles of gas.

sections.title: Reversible Reactions
sections.text: A reversible reaction can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions simultaneously, represented by the ⇌ symbol.
points: ⇌ symbol — indicates a reversible reaction that can go in both directions
Forward and reverse reactions — both occur simultaneously in a closed system
Dynamic equilibrium — forward rate = reverse rate; concentrations are constant but NOT necessarily equal
Closed system — no substances enter or leave; equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system
Position of equilibrium — describes whether more product or more reactant is present at equilibrium
Real example — N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ (colourless ⇌ brown); colour shows where equilibrium lies

sections.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
sections.text: If the conditions of a system at equilibrium are changed, the equilibrium shifts to oppose that change.
points: Increase temperature → shifts towards endothermic direction (absorbs the extra heat)
Decrease temperature → shifts towards exothermic direction (releases more heat)
Increase pressure → shifts towards side with fewer moles of gas (reduces pressure)
Decrease pressure → shifts towards side with more moles of gas
Increase concentration of a substance → equilibrium shifts away from that substance to use it up
Catalyst → equilibrium reached faster but position is UNCHANGED

sections.title: Industrial Applications — The Haber Process
sections.text: The Haber process uses equilibrium principles to manufacture ammonia as a compromise between yield and rate.
points: Equation — N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (forward reaction is exothermic)
Pressure used — 200 atm; high pressure favours right side (4 mol gas → 2 mol gas)
Temperature used — 450°C; low temp gives better yield but slower rate; 450°C is a compromise
Catalyst — iron; speeds up reaching equilibrium but does not change position
Recycling unreacted gases — N₂ and H₂ that don't react are recycled back into the reactor
Yield at 450°C — only about 15% ammonia in equilibrium mixture, but rate is acceptable

keyTerms.def: A reaction that can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions, shown by the ⇌ symbol
A state in a closed system where the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and concentrations remain constant
If conditions of a system at equilibrium are changed, the equilibrium shifts to oppose that change
Describes whether more reactants or more products are present at equilibrium
A system where no matter can enter or leave — required for equilibrium to be established
Industrial manufacture of ammonia: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, using iron catalyst at 450°C and 200 atm

examTips: Catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium but does NOT shift the position — it speeds up both forward and reverse equally.
Changing pressure only affects equilibrium if there are DIFFERENT numbers of gas moles on each side of the equation. Count them carefully.
'Dynamic' means both reactions are still occurring at equal rates — NOT that no reaction is taking place.
In the Haber process, explain why 450°C is used rather than a lower temperature: a lower temperature gives higher yield but too slow a rate; 450°C is the compromise.
commonMistakes: Saying a catalyst shifts the equilibrium position — it does not; it only speeds up reaching equilibrium.
Confusing dynamic equilibrium (reactions still occurring in both directions) with no reaction happening.
Saying concentrations are equal at equilibrium — they are constant (unchanging) but not necessarily the same as each other.
clozePassages: In a reversible reaction, products can react to reform the original reactants. When the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction in a closed system, dynamic equilibrium is reached. At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, but both reactions are still occurring. The position of equilibrium indicates whether there are more reactants or products present.

Le Chatelier's principle states that if conditions are changed, the equilibrium will shift to oppose that change. Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Increasing concentration of reactants shifts it towards products. Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas. This principle is used in industrial processes to maximise the yield of products.

The Haber process is an industrial application of equilibrium. Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. The reaction is exothermic. High pressure favours the forward reaction (fewer moles of gas on the right). Low temperature favours the forward reaction but slows the rate. A compromise temperature of 450°C and pressure of 200 atm is used, along with an iron catalyst to increase the rate.
